newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish C/A seen turning to deficit by end 1996.
newsitem.headline: Polish C/A seen turning to deficit by end 1996.

text.p: Poland's merchandise trade gap by the end of 1996 is seen growing too large to be offset by unofficial cross-border trade, which has kept the country's current account roughly balanced this year, analysts said.

They said that while cross-border trade has been practically flat in the first eight months of this year against the same period of 1995, the merchandise trade gap ballooned six-fold on the back of a 30 percent import growth rate.

In the January-August period the current account (C/A) showed a $48 million surplus, as a $4.9 billion inflow from cross-border shoppers offset a nearly $4.5 billion trade gap increased by service and interest payment outflows.
"A balanced C/A is not likely to continue, and by the end of the year Poland should have a deficit," Adam Czyzewski, economist at the independent NOBE institute told Reuters.

"Cross-border trade inflows have remained flat in nominal terms while the trade gap is rapidly widening," Czyzewski said. Analysts expect the merchandise trade deficit to balloon to around $7 billion in December from a $2.1 billion gap in 1995, against expected cross-border inflows of around $6 billion.
"If the present situation remains, the 1996 trade gap will be a minimum of $7 billion," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at the Planning Ministry.

Analysts said slow growth of the German economy, Poland's top trading partner, has curbed demand for Polish exports and dwindled their growth rate to six percent in the January-August period, according to central bank figures released on Monday.
They said even small demand fluctuations in Germany, which accounts for more than a third of Polish foreign trade, had a large impact on exports, because of their structure.

"Polish exports to developed countries, such as Germany, are largely comprised of raw materials and by-products for which demand often fluctutates more than for finished goods," Planning Ministry's Chroscicki said.

High imports growth is partly consumer-driven and last week the central bank said it wanted real interest rates to rise in the comming months to slow growth of credit action and the growth of domestic demand.
Lending to non-financial institutions grew nearly seven percent from August 1 to September 20 and by 24 percent since the start of the year against a 17.4 percent rise in broad money supply.
The growth rate was highest among household lending, which rose 64.5 percent since the end of 1995.

Analysts said that although concise figures were not available, investment imports continued to make up a large part of Polish imports, but they said a growth impulse in consumption imports was noticed in recent months.
